assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on the magic-wavelength idea, turned neutral atoms into clocks with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They allow stringent tests of fundamental physics, resolve relativistic time dilation over millimetre height differences, and are the basis for a redefinition of the second. This is precision atomic physics at its best: a clear idea, close agreement between theory and experiment, and a large payoff nobody could have foreseen at the start.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group at JILA took the scheme to record accuracy and to many-body clock physics. The two-name configuration is clean and the credit is not seriously disputed, as far as I know. Ion-clock work and the frequency-comb work honoured in 2005 are separate achievements.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced and improved in many laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good because the redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 quantum-control prizes.
Whether two names fairly represent the strontium, ytterbium and other clock communities; I am relying on memory for the detailed priority history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) picture explains the high-harmonic plateau and underpins attosecond science, strong-field ionization and orbital imaging. It is the conceptual core of the field whose experimental pulse generation the 2023 prize recognised. Its central message, that an electron driven by a strong field returns and recombines coherently with its parent ion, was unexpected and is simple to explain with a picture.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's semiclassical model (1993) is the decisive idea and the Lewenstein et al. strong-field-approximation theory (1994) supplies the quantum formulation. Kulander and Schafer's contemporaneous work is not among the supplied names, which is a possible fairness question. The two-name configuration is coherent.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many laboratories and by quantitative theory over three decades; very mature. Recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 prize. My close ties to the Lund attosecond community may call for caution or recusal, and I flag this openly.
Credit for early theory (Kulander, Schafer) falls outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought cavity QED to superconducting circuits, with strong coupling, dispersive readout and the architecture of superconducting quantum processors. It extends the 2025 theme of macroscopic quantum circuits and again asks how large a system can behave quantum mechanically.
assessment.attribution: Blais et al. (2004) is the theory proposal, Wallraff et al. (2004) the strong-coupling demonstration, and Schoelkopf's group developed the readout and device refinements, including the transmon. The three names look coherent, but Yale, Delft and others overlap in important ways.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and now the dominant platform, so mature. The risk is that it looks like a continuation of 2025.
uncertainties: Whether transmon and device engineering, rather than circuit QED itself, is the decisive contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging and quantum simulation of many-body physics. It provides a clean setting in which many-body theory and experiment can be compared closely.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller proposal (Jaksch is not among the credited names) and the Greiner-Bloch Mott experiments are the key points, with Esslinger's fermionic work and Cirac's theory also important. Five names are credited, so any three-person selection leaves out essential contributors.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely and now routine, so the experimental basis is mature. Claims of quantum-simulation advantage are still developing.
uncertainties: Allocation among five names is genuinely hard.
Overlap with earlier AMO prizes (2001, 2012) and with candidate B025.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for gravimetry, tests of the equivalence principle and measurement of constants, so it addresses fundamental questions about quantum mechanics and gravity. It is a natural complement to the laser-cooling prizes.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of atom-light interferometers, Pritchard's early atom interferometers and the Kasevich-Chu gravimeter are all decisive. The three-name selection is plausible, but priority among several early groups is delicate and Holger Müller's precision work came later. Chu already holds a prize.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and in use in metrology, but the biggest fundamental-physics results are still in progress, so recognition could be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Priority among early work from several groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light beats the standard quantum limit and is now used in gravitational-wave detectors. It is a direct illustration of quantum mechanics improving a real instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves' 1981 proposal is the theoretical origin, Kimble's group made early squeezed-state demonstrations, and Mavalvala brought it into LIGO. Slusher, Walls and others made independent early contributions, so a three-person selection is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Validated in LIGO and other detector operation. Its link to the already honoured 2017 prize may reduce the sense of novelty.
uncertainties: Credit for the early experiments is unresolved among several groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a field of correlated and superconducting moire matter with unexpected behaviour, and a theoretical prediction preceded the experiment. It is genuinely surprising, although I defer to colleagues in condensed matter for a full evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulating and superconducting states. Younger experimentalists who carried out the first measurements are outside the supplied credit, a notable fairness gap.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups, but the mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled.
The role of the experimental team in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect created a class of quantum matter with robust edge states and wide influence in condensed matter, with precise quantised transport in the HgTe experiments.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theory, and Molenkamp's group the experimental confirmation. The HgTe proposal by other theorists is not among the credited names, and the three-dimensional work makes allocation among four names nontrivial.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed independently, with mature theory and experiment. The field was already recognised in part by the 2016 topological-phases prize.
uncertainties: Contributors to the HgTe proposal are outside the supplied credit.
